cues.title: The hidden arrangement
cues.narration: Why six? Johannes Kepler asked that question in sixteen eleven. He wondered whether the geometry of packing small things together might have something to do with it. Centuries later, X-rays gave researchers a way to investigate the structure inside ice. The repeating arrangement of molecules, rather than the outline alone, was something they could now test.

cues.narration: Physicists describe the surface response with an attachment coefficient. In the growth law we are following, it tells us how effective attachment is compared with the kinetic limit. A hungry surface with a poor supply can grow slowly, just as a reluctant surface can grow slowly even when plenty of vapour is available.

captions.text: We have also seen how people made the questions measurable: grow a crystal under chosen conditions, read its dimensions, interpret an optical signal, repeat.
The resulting descriptions are not all the same kind of knowledge. Some relationships are established physical machinery.
Some numbers are inferred through a model. Some curves are fitted summaries. Some molecular explanations remain hypotheses.

cues.title: What a model chooses
cues.narration: Turning those ingredients into a model requires choices about what to represent. Heat must be carried away as ice forms; falling changes transport; the surface can be more complicated than a single effective rule. A model may omit a process, simplify it, or capture part of its influence in fitted inputs. Those choices need assessment wherever someone wants to make a quantitative claim.
cues.description: Three columns: REPRESENTED, SIMPLIFIED, OMITTED. Use examples as choices a model must state, not a falsely complete inventory. Unassessed effects read EFFECT NOT YET BOUNDED.

cues.narration: This is not a reason to give up on the equations. It is a reason to ask them a clear question and compare the answer with observations. A model that draws a beautiful crystal has accomplished something. A model that predicts the right growth under specified conditions has accomplished something more demanding. We need a test that can tell those achievements apart.

cues.title: One crystal, several questions
cues.narration: Before we return to the computer, look once more at the kind of crystal we set out to understand. Its six directions connect to a lattice. Its branching connects to an unstable growth front and an uneven supply. Its overall proportions lead us back to the relative behaviour of its faces. These are different questions occupying the same small piece of ice.

cues.title: The wonder becomes specific
cues.narration: A finished crystal can also suggest a history, although it does not hand us a complete record of the weather. And at its growing surface, familiar water is doing things the models still describe imperfectly. The wonder has not disappeared as we learned more. It has become more specific: particular structures, particular measurements, and particular questions that an experiment might answer.
